titulo: Designing a good tool: name, description, JSON Schema, idempotency, read-only × with consequences
lead: The model picks the tool by reading its name, description, and schema. The client decides whether to ask for approval by reading the annotations. A badly designed tool gets called at the wrong time or with the wrong argument. In this lesson, you use a script to check that your tools say what they do and what they change.
objetivo: write the name, description, schema, and annotations that let the agent choose correctly and let the client ask for confirmation when there are consequences.

aprende.t: One intent per tool, with a name and description that state it
An input schema that rejects the wrong argument before your code runs
The four annotations, and the default when you say nothing
Text and structured results; an error the model can read

hero_alt: A dark workbench with precision tools lined up, each with a blank label, one with a red lock.

secoes.titulo: What the model and the client read
secoes.sub: Click each part of a tool's registration.

nos.detalhe: Start from the person's journey ("find a class with a seat"), not from the name of a function in your code. Two tools that answer the same request make the model guess.
Short and with a verb: buscar_turmas, reservar_vaga. The title is the label for people; the name is what the model calls.
It says what the tool does, when to use it, and whether it has consequences. It's the only explanation the model gets, along with the description of each argument.
Zod becomes JSON Schema 2020-12 in tools/list. The SDK validates before the handler: an argument outside the schema comes back as isError and your code doesn't even run.

readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint. The client uses them to decide whether to approve on its own or ask. They are hints: they don't change execution, and a client shouldn't trust them when they come from an unknown server.
content for the model to read and, with outputSchema, structuredContent validated by the SDK before it goes out.

secoes.legenda: Annotation semantics per the ToolAnnotations type in the 2026-07-28 revision (official SDK code, 10/13/2026).

secoes.sub: The specification's defaults apply when you omit the annotation.

texto: true = the tool doesn't change the environment. A host can approve a read-only tool on its own.
Without the annotation, the client should assume it changes something.
Only makes sense when the tool is not read-only. true = can delete or overwrite; false = only adds (like a new booking).
If you leave it out on a tool that changes something, the client treats it as destructive.
true = repeating the call with the same arguments has no extra effect. It matters because clients retry calls (the network dropped, MRTR in lesson 5).
reservar_vaga is not idempotent: two calls, two seats.
true = talks to the outside world (web search, third-party API). false = closed domain, like the kit's in-memory catalog.
An open-world tool is an entry point for untrusted content: course 4 covers this.

The termo "m" has 1 character and the schema asks for 2: the SDK rejected it and returned the message as a result with isError, which the model reads and fixes.

exercicios.titulo: E7 · Make it fail on purpose
exercicios.texto: Delete the annotations line from buscar_turmas and run it again. Then put the line back.
exercicios.pronto: without the line: FALHA buscar_turmas: diz se é só leitura and saída: 1; with the line back: 0 falhas.

exercicios.titulo: E8 · A tool for your service
exercicios.texto: Pick a tool from your mapa-mcp.md (lesson 1) and register it in servidor.mjs with a description, a schema with limits, and the four annotations.
exercicios.pronto: node teste-ferramentas.mjs → 0 falhas with your tool listed in the ok lines.

perguntas.p: You registered a tool that deletes records and forgot the annotations. How should the client treat it?
opcoes: As read-only, because nothing was said
As able to change things and to destroy them
perguntas.explica: The defaults are readOnlyHint false and destructiveHint true. Leaving them out doesn't make the tool safer: it makes the client more cautious, which is right.

perguntas.p: The model calls buscar_turmas with termo "m". What happens?
opcoes: The handler runs and returns an empty list
The SDK rejects it by the schema and returns isError
The server crashes and the client reconnects
The client blocks the call before sending it
perguntas.explica: The schema asks for at least 2 characters. The SDK validates before the handler and returns the message as a result with isError, which the model reads.

opcoes: Because it talks to an external service
Because it returns text, not structured data
Because each repeated call books one more seat
Because it requires an email in the schema
perguntas.explica: Idempotent means repeating has no extra effect. Two identical bookings take two seats, so the client should not blindly retry.

perguntas.p: Which of these is the best description for a tool?
opcoes: Books a seat for the email; has consequences and asks for confirmation
The reservar function from the scheduling module
Makes bookings and other useful things in the system
perguntas.explica: It says what it does, on what, and that it has consequences. "Manages" and "other things" make the model guess when to call it.

itens.texto: One per tool; a name with a verb; a description that warns about the consequence.
Limits in Zod: the SDK rejects before your code runs.
State all four; omitting = destructive to the client.
